analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 30% minimum tax on income above $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill to make households earning over $1 million pay at least a 30% tax rate never received a committee hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone with income over $1 million a year to pay a minimum tax of 30% on that income, after allowing a deduction for charitable giving. It would apply on top of the regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes, so no amount of tax breaks, capital-gains rates, or loopholes could push a millionaire's rate below the floor. It would also phase in gradually for incomes just above $1 million and adjust the threshold for inflation. The bill was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, everyone else who pays federal taxes would benefit from the additional revenue — the bill's own text says it would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year. The direct beneficiaries are taxpayers earning under $1 million, who would face no new tax, along with anyone who benefits from deficit reduction. It would also raise effective rates on very high-income households who currently pay low rates because much of their income is taxed at capital-gains rates or sheltered by deductions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires individuals with adjusted gross income over $1 million to pay a minimum tax equal to 30% of income above the charitable-deduction allowance, so their total federal rate cannot fall below that floor no matter what deductions or special rates they use.

The tax applies in addition to regular income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes, and it is reduced only by those existing liabilities — meaning preferential rates on investment income can no longer bring a millionaire's effective rate below 30%.
The bill states it is designed to serve as a floor on taxes for the highest-income taxpayers and to cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year while encouraging broader tax reform.
It includes a phase-in so taxpayers just over the $1 million threshold pay a partial rate, and the threshold adjusts with inflation after 2023 so it does not sweep in more people over time.

analysis.who_pays: Households with annual income over $1 million — roughly the top fraction of one percent of taxpayers — would pay more, particularly those whose income comes largely from investments taxed at lower rates or who use deductions to shrink their taxable income. The bill leaves untouched anyone below the threshold.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to all income above the threshold regardless of its source, so a household with an unusually large one-time gain — for example, selling a family business or farm after years of ordinary income — could owe the minimum tax in that year even if its typical income is far lower, since the threshold adjusts only for inflation and there is no averaging provision.

Charitable giving is only partially protected: non-itemizers get no charitable deduction at all against the fair share tax, and itemizers get a reduced one, which would raise the after-tax cost of giving for some large donors and could reduce charitable donations.

Raising the minimum rate on investment income increases the cost of capital for the businesses and ventures that very high-income households finance, which supporters would have to weigh against the revenue gained.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a modestly higher tax bill for a small number of very high-income households in exchange for billions in deficit reduction spread across everyone else. The design flaws worth acknowledging are the one-time-income problem — a household can cross the threshold in a single year from selling an asset — and the partial charitable-deduction carve-out. Neither undermines the main effect, which is to close the gap that lets the highest earners pay lower rates than middle-income workers on the same dollar of income. The bill's main weakness is not its design but its fate: it never received even a committee hearing, so no one had to vote on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025, without a hearing, a markup, or any floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Paying a Fair Share Act on April 18, 2023, with 14 other Senate Democrats as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.

The bill's entire action history consists of that introduction and referral; no hearing, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing.
Its 15 Senate supporters were all Democrats or allied independents; no Republican cosponsored it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with income over $1 million are better off: they keep the lower effective rates the bill would have eliminated, and they paid nothing in the way of new organizing or lobbying because the bill never got a hearing. The Finance Committee was never required to take a position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Million-dollar earners kept lower tax rates

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse

for.name: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 18, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: None of the 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, and the committee to which it was referred took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call; its only recorded support was 15 Democrats and independents, with none of the 49 Senate Republicans backing it.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on this group, which currently can pay lower effective rates than middle-income earners because much of its income is taxed at capital-gains rates or sheltered by deductions. Its interest in the bill's failure runs directly against the taxpayers who would benefit from the revenue.

industries.industry: Hedge fund and private equity managers
industries.note: These firms earn much of their income through preferential carried-interest and capital-gains rates; a 30% floor on high earners' total tax bill would sharply reduce the value of those rates. Their interest in keeping those rates runs against ordinary wage earners, who pay payroll tax on every dollar.

industries.industry: Tax planning and wealth management services
industries.note: A significant business exists to restructure high earners' income so it is taxed at lower rates; a hard 30% floor would make much of that work pointless. The public's interest in simpler, harder-to-game taxation runs against that business model.
